Seminar Title:

Beyond the Forests: Ecotourism and Sustainable Livelihoods in the Protected Landscapes of Karnataka, India

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Humanities and Social Sciences

Speaker Name:

Sachin C Pujar ( Rollno : 518hs1009)

Speaker Type:

Venue:

HS Seminar Room (MN 436)

Koteswara Rao Kodirekkala

Abstract:

Ecotourism has been advocated across the world as a strategy to reconcile biodiversity conservation with community livelihood goals in and around protected areas however, the extent to which ecotourism delivers on these promises remains contested. The present study investigates the nature and impact of ecotourism on sustainable livelihoods in two protected landscapes of Karnataka- the Kali Tiger Reserve (KTR) and the Nagarahole Tiger Reserve (NTR) both reserves operate under an identical state and national policy framework and are managed by the same Forest Department yet have delivered dramatically different outcomes for their host communities. This research is grounded in anthropology and tourism studies and draws on three interrelated theoretical perspectives: The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework Bryant&rsquos framework of Political Ecology of the Third World and Stakeholder Collaboration Theory incorporating the Pretty Tosun typology of participation. The study utilised a comparative mixed methods approach, using data from 503 participants consisting of 214 local community residents (KTR = 100 NTR = 114) 200 visitors to the reserves (100 per site) and 89 tourism operators/owners (KTR = 55 NTR = 34). In addition, qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, quasi participant observation and case studies as well as institutional records.

The findings of the research revealed two structurally distinct models of ecotourism operating in the study areas, namely embedded (KTR) and enclave (NTR) ecotourism. Embedded ecotourism in KTR exists where the community and is embedded within the existing economy, where some intermediaries (such as Eco-Development Committees and Village Forest Committees) mediate the flow of economic benefit from tourists to the local economy. The embedded nature of ecotourism within the KTR involves local entrepreneurs owning their own accommodation units (homestays), which creates opportunities for a broader spread of households to receive some economic benefit, albeit at a limited scale. Enclave ecotourism in NTR represents a separate entity, operating outside of the local economy. The enclave consists of large-scale luxury resorts operated by external owners who employ local workers primarily in low-skilled roles. The majority of surplus created in these operations leaves the local economy. The divergence between the two models was determined through examination of four interdependent factors namely, the historical context of dispossession the institutional capacity of the local economy the level of tourist development potential available to the area and the type of visitors that the two areas attract. Counterintuitively, it was observed that the area hosting the more prestigious and profitable tourism product had the poorer of the two local populations. Neither model meets the social and cultural objectives associated with ecotourism. The two reserves converge in their social outcomes: participation remains passive at both sites, respondents in each perceive the allocation of employment as inequitable, and local culture is largely absent from the tourism product on offer. The study&rsquos central conclusion is that the livelihood outcomes of ecotourism are not dependent on tourism revenue, visitor volume, or natural endowment, but on the presence or absence of a functioning, locally embedded intermediary institution capable of converting community participation into benefits that the community retains and controls.

Based on these results, the study has suggested policy interventions for protected areas in Karnataka, such as an institutional revival of eco-development committees and village forest committees a regulatory definition of ecotourism separating the functionally contradictory roles of the Forest Department protecting homestays at the local level and linking tourism to existing livelihoods to reduce seasonal variability. These findings also add to debates around participation in nature-conservation and community-based tourism, while providing a transferable conceptual distinction between &lsquoembedded&rsquo and &lsquoenclave&rsquo ecotourism that can be used by researchers working on tourism in protected landscapes.

Keywords: Ecotourism protected areas sustainable livelihoods community participation Karnataka
